title: The TLS Protocol Version 1.0
summary: Specifies version 1.0 of Transport Layer Security, which gives communications privacy over the Internet. It is designed so client and server programs can talk in a way that prevents eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 4346.

plainLanguage.summary: TLS 1.0 defines how two applications negotiate security settings and protect data sent over a reliable transport. It was later replaced by TLS 1.1 in RFC 4346.

questions: how does tls protect internet traffic
how does the tls handshake work
what is the tls record protocol
subtitle: The first TLS specification for privacy and data integrity between applications.

tldr.problem: Applications communicating across a network need privacy and data integrity without each protocol defining its own security mechanisms.
tldr.mechanism: TLS 1.0 combines a Record Protocol that protects data with a Handshake Protocol that negotiates algorithms, authenticates peers, and establishes shared keys.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2246 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 4346. It was also updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 2246 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 4346. It was also updated by RFC 3546, RFC 5746, RFC 6176, RFC 7465, RFC 7507, and RFC 7919.

sections.title: TLS Goals and Structure
sections.content:
TLS aims to provide privacy and data integrity between two applications. Its Record Protocol runs over a reliable transport and uses symmetric cryptography to encrypt data and a keyed message authentication code to check integrity.

The Handshake Protocol lets peers authenticate and negotiate a shared secret and algorithms. TLS is independent of the application protocol, while the application designers decide how and when to start a handshake.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS protects data exchanged between applications. The endpoints first negotiate keys and security settings, then the record layer uses those settings to protect the data.

sections.title: The Record Protocol
sections.content:
The Record Protocol fragments data, may compress it, adds an integrity check, encrypts it, and sends it. A receiver decrypts and checks the record before decompressing and reassembling the data.

Each record carries a content type, version, length, and fragment. The protocol uses connection state and sequence numbers when calculating the integrity check, which helps detect records that are missing, repeated, or changed.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS divides data into records and protects each record before sending it. The receiver checks each record and restores the original data for the application.

sections.title: The Handshake Protocol
sections.content:
The client starts by sending a ClientHello with supported protocol and cryptographic options. The server responds with a ServerHello selecting parameters and may send a certificate and key-exchange information.

The client and server exchange further handshake messages to establish shared keys and verify that the negotiation was not changed. A session identifier can allow a later connection to resume a session with an abbreviated handshake.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server exchange hello messages to select compatible settings. They then establish shared keys and confirm the handshake before application data is sent.

sections.title: Alerts and Closing
sections.content:
TLS alert messages carry a warning or fatal level and a description of the condition. A fatal alert ends the connection. The RFC defines alerts for protocol errors and handshake failures.

A party sends close_notify before closing its sending side. This tells the other party that the data stream ended deliberately.
sections.plainLanguage: An alert reports a problem, and a fatal alert ends the connection. The close_notify message tells the peer that the sender has finished normally.

sections.title: Cipher Suites and Security Analysis
sections.content:
The RFC requires compliant applications to implement a specified cipher suite unless an application profile says otherwise. Its security analysis discusses authentication, key exchange, rollback attacks, session resumption, and protection of application data.

The RFC explains that unauthenticated key exchange is vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack. It also warns that an attacker may try to force peers to use weaker options, so applications must apply their own security requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS security depends on the negotiated algorithms and on authenticating at least one peer. The RFC warns that applications must not accept weaker protection than their needs allow.
